reason: Wording held against the named translation as far as it can be reached. The Knopf 1990 scans on archive.org (disturbingpeacec00have, disturbingpeacec00have_0) are lending restricted and refused a search-inside this run, so the page itself was not seen. But archive.org full-text search returns dozens of independent printings that quote the two sentences identically, including The New Republic introducing them as from Disturbing the Peace and an Advent 2005 reader naming the book, and the PMC article (fetched this run) gives Knopf 1990, trans. Paul Wilson, p. 181. The only variants in the wild drop the comma before regardless (quotation books); the Wilson reading with the comma is the majority and the scholarly one. Attribution is right: Havel speaks in his own voice, and the answers were written, not spoken, in 1985 to 1986, so it is the page and not the podium; nothing on the misattribution list touches it. shipped.js: not shipped, no near opening, Havel 0 of 3, not banned. In scope (Czech 1986, English 1990), publishable, ends in a full stop, prose kept as prose. Source line is 69 characters, leads with the name, no dash; adding the publisher makes the edition locatable, hence the betterCitation. Three soft points for the editor, none a refutation: (1) the same line is proposed by the fiction-essay lane as 12-fict-14, so only one of the two ids may land; (2) that lane tags it Essay, and the form of the work is a book-length written interview, which is closer to Essay than Philosophy; (3) p. 181 is the page for these two sentences, the Havel Center range pp. 181 to 182 covers the whole answer.
